strengths: PST addresses a relevant gap in language-conditioned image generation: depicting two people can expose different stereotype patterns from single-person prompts. Counterbalancing left/right order and examining organizational roles within occupations are useful design choices. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b01/review-experiment-66wktdty/call-ca33e70141294d7fb93670900c2a6a95/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The occupation-level results support a meaningful descriptive finding: DALL-E 3's adherence to male occupational stereotypes increases substantially under paired prompts. The detailed tables make this pattern inspectable.

Three annotators per image and reported Fleiss' kappa values of 0.88–0.92 support reliable perceived-gender labeling. The appendices provide occupation lists, generation templates, and annotation instructions. FairCritic offers a practical mitigation idea with promising reported score reductions.
weaknesses: The central fairness claims exceed what the signed Stereotype Score establishes. Opposing disparities can cancel: Table 1's single-person occupational score of 10 combines female-stereotype SS of 50 and male-stereotype SS of −30. Neither a small aggregate score nor the two broad gender strata establishes parity for individual occupations. FairCritic needs results showing absolute deviations from parity by occupation and role before claiming 'near-perfect fairness.' Figure 6 also compares different events: independently balanced binary gender assignments would produce at least one stereotype-adhering person in 75% of paired images, so the headline 74% statistic alone is not evidence of unfairness.

The single-person baseline uses only three images per identity, making occupation-level estimates and rankings highly unstable. No confidence intervals or uncertainty analysis accompany the comparisons, and occupational PST has only one generation run. More baseline samples and uncertainty estimates that account for shared occupations and paired subjects are needed to establish the reliability of the reported differences.

The evaluation does not report validation that generated subjects actually exhibit the requested occupations, organizational roles, or left/right placement. High agreement on gender appearance does not validate those role assignments. Handling of 'Cannot Identify' responses, annotation disagreements, and invalid generations is also unspecified.

FairCritic is insufficiently specified to reproduce its reported results. Section 5.1 lacks the complete critic configuration, image batch sizes, operational bias criterion, feedback application procedure, and final evaluation sample counts. The schematic and named model are insufficient substitutes, while code and data are only promised for release. These omissions and the measurement concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

The mitigation comparison does not isolate the contribution of adaptive visual feedback. The occupational intervention baseline uses the five most biased occupations per gender, whereas FairCritic's principal results cover the full set. Evaluation on identical prompts, an ablation using fixed feedback, and a simple balanced-gender prompting baseline would clarify the claimed advantage. Testing one substantive generator also limits broader claims about T2I systems.

Reporting inconsistencies require reconciliation. The prompt inventory alternates between 944 and 1,952. In Table 1, FairCritic's organizational-power subgroup scores, 11.40 and −1.96, average to 4.72 rather than the reported 5.09; any unequal weighting or exclusions need explanation. Exact evaluated counts and aggregation rules are necessary for auditing the results.
